claims.text: A high density of undercoordinated defect sites on Pt nanoparticles enhances activity in ethanol oxidation.
A high density of undercoordinated defect sites on Pt nanoparticles improves selectivity for complete ethanol oxidation.
A high density of undercoordinated defect sites on Pt nanoparticles enhances catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
Undercoordinated surface atoms modify the adsorption or binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Defect sites lower activation barriers for C–C bond cleavage during ethanol oxidation on Pt.
Defect sites lower activation barriers for C–H bond cleavage during ethanol oxidation on Pt.
Ethanol oxidation is a 12-electron and 12-proton transfer reaction.
Conventional thermal annealing yields well-faceted Pt nanoparticles with low surface-defect density.
Ultrafast laser ablation or controlled milling can generate steps, twin boundaries, and vacancies on Pt nanoparticles while preserving similar particle size and composition.
An increased surface-defect density yields more undercoordinated atoms and altered local coordination environments.
Surface defects alter the local electronic structure of Pt nanoparticles.
Defect-induced changes in intermediate binding and activation barriers can enhance oxidation electrokinetics.
Stabilization of key intermediates by Pt defects facilitates complete ethanol oxidation.
Defect-mediated changes in intermediate binding reduce catalyst poisoning.
Reduced catalyst poisoning increases durability under repeated electrochemical cycling.
Higher-defect Pt catalysts will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current densities than well-faceted Pt catalysts.
Higher-defect Pt catalysts will form fewer partial ethanol-oxidation products.
The defect-mediated mechanism should apply under room-temperature electrochemical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Extreme potentials, abnormal pH, or oxide-dominated operation can limit the explanatory power of the defect-mediated mechanism.
Failure to observe improved performance or a defect-density/performance correlation would falsify the proposed governing role of surface defects.
